summary: In this episode, the hosts discuss the sacrament of the consecration of kings and emperors, tracing its origins from the Old Testament concept of kingship as an icon of God's rule, through the Byzantine coronation rite, and into the modern context. They explore how kingship is rooted in Genesis and the covenant structure, with the king serving as a vassal of the Great King, God. The episode debunks myths about Constantine, including his conversion, the Council of Nicaea, and his coronation, and examines the relationship between church and state, particularly the concept of symphonia. The hosts conclude by applying these ancient principles to contemporary political life, emphasizing the importance of community and the hope found in Christ as the true King.

entities.title: Constantine the Great
entities.summary: Roman Emperor (r. 306-337) who converted to Christianity, legalized Christianity, and convened the First Council of Nicaea.

entities.title: King Charles III
entities.summary: Current King of the United Kingdom, whose coronation anointing oil was blessed by the Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem.

entities.title: Eusebius of Caesarea
entities.summary: Early church historian and bishop, a contemporary of Constantine, whose writings are a key source for Constantine's life.

entities.title: Lactantius
entities.summary: Early Christian author who wrote an account of Constantine's vision before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge.

entities.title: Saul (King of Israel)
entities.summary: First king of Israel, whose failure to obey God led to his rejection; an example of a king who acted as a priest-king illegitimately.

entities.title: David (King of Israel)
entities.summary: Second king of Israel, a model of kingship as an icon of God, and a type of the Messiah.

entities.title: Julius Caesar
entities.summary: Roman general and dictator whose assassination marked the end of the Roman Republic and the rise of the Empire.

entities.title: Augustus (Octavian)
entities.summary: First Roman Emperor, who succeeded where Julius Caesar failed in establishing the Empire.

entities.title: Peter the Great
entities.summary: Russian Tsar who abolished the patriarchate and subjugated the church to the state, influencing later coronation practices.

entities.title: Ignatius of Smolensk
entities.summary: Russian traveler who witnessed and recorded the coronation of Byzantine Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos.

entities.title: Manuel II Palaiologos
entities.summary: Byzantine Emperor (r. 1391-1425) whose coronation was described by Ignatius of Smolensk.

entities.title: Pontius Pilate
entities.summary: Roman governor who condemned Jesus to crucifixion; Jesus told him that his authority came from above.

entities.title: St. Paul
entities.summary: Apostle who wrote Romans 13, teaching that governing authorities are instituted by God and are His servants.

entities.title: St. Gregory of Nyssa
entities.summary: Church Father who preached against slavery, saying it was wrong to own another person created in the image of Christ.

entities.title: Theodosius I
entities.summary: Roman Emperor who made Christianity the official religion of the empire, about 70 years after Constantine.

entities.title: Julian the Apostate
entities.summary: Roman Emperor who attempted to restore paganism after Constantine's Christianization.

entities.title: Nestorius
entities.summary: Archbishop of Constantinople who objected to the Empress receiving communion in the sanctuary, leading to controversy.

entities.title: Theotokos
entities.summary: The Virgin Mary, Mother of God; the Empress defended her entrance into the sanctuary by referencing the Theotokos entering the temple.

entities.title: Roman Empire
entities.summary: The empire that Constantine ruled and Christianized, which became the model for Christian kingship.

entities.title: Byzantine Empire
entities.summary: The Eastern Roman Empire, which continued the Christian imperial tradition after the fall of the West.

entities.title: Council of Nicaea
entities.summary: First Ecumenical Council convened by Constantine in 325 AD, which addressed Arianism and established the Nicene Creed.

entities.title: Edict of Milan
entities.summary: Edict issued by Constantine and Licinius in 313 AD that legalized Christianity and restored confiscated property.

entities.title: Battle of Milvian Bridge
entities.summary: Battle in 312 AD where Constantine defeated Maxentius, after which he became sole emperor of the West.

entities.title: Chi-Rho
entities.summary: A Christian symbol formed by superimposing the first two letters of 'Christ' in Greek, which Constantine was told to put on his soldiers' shields.

concepts.title: Kingship as Icon
concepts.summary: The concept that the king serves as an icon of God's rule, both representing God to the people and being venerated by them, but not worshipped as a god.

concepts.title: Symphonia
concepts.summary: The Byzantine concept of church and state working in harmony, with the emperor and patriarch having distinct but complementary ministries.

concepts.title: Coronation as Sacrament
concepts.summary: The anointing and crowning of a king or emperor is a sacramental act, conferring a ministry and office from God, similar to ordination.

concepts.title: Divine Right of Kings
concepts.summary: The idea that a king's authority comes directly from God, but this does not mean the king is above accountability; rather, it entails greater responsibility.

concepts.title: Separation of Church and State
concepts.summary: A modern concept that did not exist in the early church; the Byzantine model saw the emperor and patriarch as partners in governing a Christian society.

claims.text: Kingship originates in Genesis, where God rests on the seventh day, meaning He is seated on His throne to preside over creation.
The Torah is patterned after ancient Near Eastern suzerain-vassal treaties, presenting God as the Great King and Israel as His vassal.
The king of Israel is a vassal of God, with specific responsibilities outlined in Deuteronomy 17, including not acquiring many horses, wives, or excessive wealth.
The Israelite king is an icon of God, not an idol like pagan kings who were worshipped as gods.
Constantine genuinely converted to Christianity, as evidenced by his actions: he stopped offering pagan sacrifices, ended gladiatorial combat, and issued laws reflecting Christian values.
The Council of Nicaea did not decide which books are in the Bible; it was not even discussed.
The Council of Nicaea did not create the Roman Catholic Church.
The Council of Nicaea did not cover up Jesus's secret family or his relationship with Mary Magdalene.
The Council of Nicaea did not change the identity of Jewish people or declare some other group to be the real Israelites.
The Council of Nicaea did not burn any books, churches, or people; Arianism continued for a century afterward.
The Council of Nicaea did not force Constantine's theology on anyone; he may have been semi-Arian himself.
The Council of Nicaea did not proclaim Jesus to be divine; that was already believed. The debate was about the nature of his divinity.
The Council of Nicaea did not move Christian worship to Sunday; Christians gathered on the Lord's Day from the New Testament era.
The Council of Nicaea did not begin the practice of baptizing babies.
The Council of Nicaea could not have ended slavery; it was not within their jurisdiction, and the economic system could not be changed by a vote.
St. Paul's plan was to preach the gospel to the emperor, and Constantine's conversion was the fulfillment of that plan.
The Byzantine emperor received communion at the altar with the clergy, signifying his office as a minister of God, not as a layperson.

scriptural_links.summary: The creation account, where God rests on the seventh day, establishing the pattern of kingship and the Sabbath.
Commandments for the future king of Israel, including not acquiring many horses, wives, or wealth, and writing a copy of the Torah.
The Ten Commandments, which follow the pattern of a suzerain-vassal treaty, beginning with God's self-identification and what He has done.
A psalm about the judgment of the gods (fallen angels) for failing to do justice, which is also the standard for judging kings.
Jesus tells Pilate that he would have no authority unless it were given from above, showing that all power is derivative.
Paul teaches that governing authorities are instituted by God and are His servants, and that we should honor them.
The heavenly worship of the Lamb, showing that Christ is the true King and the one worthy of all honor.

glossary.definition: Anointing oil used in sacraments, including the anointing of kings and emperors.
An ancient Near Eastern treaty form where a great king makes a covenant with a lesser king, including historical prologue, stipulations, blessings, and curses.
Latin title meaning 'commander' or 'conqueror,' which became the basis for the title 'emperor.'
The title of the Roman Emperor as the high priest of the Roman state religion, responsible for offering sacrifices.
The council of nobles and bishops in Anglo-Saxon England who elected the king.
The elevated platform in a church from which the gospel is read and where the emperor was anointed and crowned.
Greek word meaning 'worthy,' chanted during ordinations and the coronation of the emperor.
The Byzantine ideal of harmony between church and state, with the emperor and patriarch working together.
